newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Asia needs private sector in infrastructure - W.Bank.
newsitem.headline: Asia needs private sector in infrastructure - W.Bank.

text.p: High initial expectations for private involvement in Asian infrastructure projects have not been met, the World Bank said on Tuesday, urging governments to provide a clear framework for private participation.

Russ Cheetham, World Bank vice-president for East Asia and the Pacific Region, told a conference of regional government and industry leaders that private participation in infrastructure projects was needed to support future growth and quality of life.

"The high expectations for private involvement have been followed by disappointments. The needs are great, but the initial momentum has stalled," he told the Frontiers of the Public-Private Interface in East Asia Infrastructure conference.

He said by one estimate, the total size of project financing accomplished in East Asia was $5 billion in 1995, of which $3 billion went to just two power projects, Paiton in Indonesia and Sual in the Philippines.
"The private sector is financing and participating in less than 10 percent of total infrastructure investment," he said.

"There is a lot of interest in power generation, but little in transmission or distribution; toll roads have experienced setbacks; and private involvement has been limited and largely opportunistic in water, despite major needs," he said.
The meeting was told private activity would inevitably start slowly in such projects, on a transaction-by-transaction basis.
"But the real gains -- to both sides -- will only occur if East Asian societies move beyond individual transactions," Cheetham said.

"The ingredients of such a framework will depend on country conditions, but it is likely that measures to reduce risks, promote competition and transparency, and avoid excessive guarantees by governments will be common elements," he said.

Indonesian Minister for National Development Planning Ginandjar Kartasasmita told the meeting that the World Bank had estimated the East Asia region needed $1.5 trillion in investment in infrastructure between 1995 and 2004.
"Needless to say, these are fantastic sums which strain both financing capacity and implementation ability," Ginandjar said.
"Without innovation, planning and acceptance of the private sector as a provider we will not succeed in achieving our regional economic growth aspirations," he said.
Ginandjar said financing was a special area of difficulty as funds from traditional banking sources were limited because of mismatches between project timetables and lender requirements.
"The projects may need 15 to 30 years to recover their investments and traditional lenders are typically not interested in more than five to 10 years at the longest," he said.

Rowena Chu, managing director of investment banking for China with the Hong Kong-based JP Morgan Securities Asia, told the conference both sides needed greater understanding to promote more private investment in infrastructure.
"The private sector needs to understand the priorities of the public sector in projects but also in the development of capital markets," Chu said.
"The public sector has to provide a clear and transparent process of approval and implementation for infrastructure projects," she added.
